extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / chymists (learned readers of early-modern chemistry)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for conducting, interpreting, and classifying chemical (chymical) experiments and products — including procedural instructions for producing and identifying volatile salts and higher-level principles about what counts as an element or cause in chymical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for producing a volatile salt (Tartari Fugitivus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take of good Antimony, Salt-Petre and Tartar, of each an equal weight, and of Quicklime half the weight of any one of them; powder and mingle; have a long-necked earth retort with a hole at the top placed in a furnace, heat till the sides are red hot, cast in the mixture by about half a spoonful at a time and stop the hole; collect condensed fumes in a receiver and rectify the liquor to a pure golden spirit; further separate salt by putting the liquor into an inclined glass egg in hot sand to sublime a fine salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact proportions and apparatus described; add mixture nimbly and stop to force fumes into receiver; expected yield: a spirit carrying a golden colour and a volatile crystalline salt. Author warns he has not fully proved the salt is pure tartar and it may include nitre or antimony impurities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic properties/tests for identifying this volatile salt
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable reactions and sensory properties that distinguish the volatile salt produced: 'saltish, not an Acid Salt'; hisses upon the affusion of Spirit of Nitre or Oyle of Vitriol; precipitates corals dissolved in Spirit of Vinager; turns the blue syrup of violets immediately green; turns the solution of Sublimate into a milky whiteness; very volatile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these qualitative chemical tests (smell, taste, effervescence, colour reactions, precipitation) to compare the product to known 'volatile salts of animals' and to judge affinity or difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation apparatus & technique as an experimental standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a long-necked earthen retort placed in a furnace for naked fire, fitted with a large receiver; heat the retort till the sides are red hot before introducing the mixture, add small portions quickly by the top-hole and stop it so fumes pass into the receiver; rectify the distilled liquor; for sublimation, use a glass egg or bolthead with a long narrow neck, inclined in hot sand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives practical steps (heating to red hot, small incremental charging, quick stopping) and apparatus forms (retort, receiver, inclined glass egg) as essential technique to obtain desired volatile spirits and sublime salts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metal–saline co-mixtures to produce distinct spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: Burying thin plates of copper in grape husks (marc) leads the saline parts to coagulate with the copper into verdigrease; distilling verdigrease in naked fire yields a distillate smelling and tasting strong like Aqua Fortis and surpassing rectified spirit of vinegar; copper remains as crocus (reddish powder) in the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting distillates requires attention to how metallic contact alters saline constituents: the distillate may be ascribed to salts altered by co‑mixture with metal rather than to pure vinegars; observe residues (crocus) to infer metallic participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational principle: products of fire are often compounded, not true simple elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When bodies are resolved by fire into supposed simple ingredients, those substances are not necessarily true, proper Elements but may be 'accidentally produc'd by the fire,' i.e., compounds or new associations brought about by the fire's dissipating action in close vessels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that distillation products equal primordial elements; interpret analytical results cautiously — the 'elements' obtained by fire can be contingent on the operation and vessel and so may be compound rather than elementary.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed universal number of elemental principles
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no necessarily determinate number (three, five, etc.) of principles universally present in all mixed bodies; analyses show that vegetable, animal, and mineral bodies may yield different counts and sorts of separable parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid commitment to quaternary, ternary, or any fixed scheme; let particular experiments determine how many salient principles a given concrete yields rather than assuming universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: some qualities (esp. medical virtues) lodge chiefly but not exclusively in one principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Divers Qualities, and especially Medical Virtues, do for the most part lodge in some One or Other of its principles, and may therefore usefully be sought for in that principle sever'd from the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pharmacological investigation, seek active virtues in separated principles but recognize they may not be exclusively or entirely localized; use separation as a heuristic for discovery, not as ontological proof of pure locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution: extraordinary chymical claims require direct observation (αυτοψια) and strong evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about matchless agents (e.g., the Alkahest) are so 'unparallell'd and stupendious' that little less than personal, eyewitness examination is requisite to be sure of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain skepticism toward extraordinary or grand claims until verified by direct, replicable observation; do not accept assertions based solely on hearsay or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended approach: learn by particular experiments; do not rely on fire alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The surest way is to learn by particular experiments what differing parts particular bodies consist of, and by what ways (either actual or potential fire) they may best and most conveniently be separated; avoid relying too much on the fire alone for resolving bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use many kinds of experiments and practical skill (a 'skilfull Artist') to probe bodies; prefer incremental, particular trials over sweeping analytical claims made from a single method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual moderation: accept practical 'elements' as convenient names while avoiding claiming them as perfectly pure
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the principles may not be perfectly devoid of mixture, they may without inconvenience be call'd the Elements of compounded bodies and bear the names of those substances which they most resemble; yet one should not strip sever'd principles so naked as to make them 'exquisitely elementary' and almost useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat elemental labels (salt, spirit, oil) as useful classificatory tools for practical work, but avoid reifying them as absolutely simple substances divorced from their experimental provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concessional classification: probable separations for minerals, vegetables, and animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Divers Mineral Bodies may be resolv'd into a Saline, a Sulphureous, and a Mercurial part; almost all Vegetable and Animal concretes may be divided (by a skilful artist) into five differing substances: Salt, Spirit, Oyle, Phlegme and Earth; of which Salt, Spirit, and Oyle are the three active principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a fair concession to chymists: a working taxonomy for separating and naming operative parts, useful for practice and for seeking virtues, though not dogmatically universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not despise earth and water; recognize the efficacy of heat and cold as agents
rubrics_metrics.description: The common practice to vilify Earth and Water because they lack 'Specifick Properties' is unjustified; Heat (an 'Elementary Quality') performs innumerable operations, and Cold can produce stupendous effects (examples: hardening or making steel brittle by sudden cooling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating elemental roles, consider the demonstrable powers of heat and cold and the operational significance of earth and water; empirical effects (e.g., quenching experiments) should inform theoretical valuation of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic critique: chymists often possess experiments but not causal explanations — require rational/experimental grounds before accepting hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Chymists have been 'much more happy in finding Experiments than the Causes of them'; experiments are numerous but analytical explanations are often unaccurate and unconcluding; one should not be content with mere experimental results without rational demonstration of the causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand both reproducible experiments and careful inference about causes; be willing to revise hypotheses when experiments are properly interpreted, and avoid adopting theories that outstrip the experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental inference: changes in distillate composition can reflect prior metal–salt interactions, not simply original liquid composition
rubrics_metrics.description: When saline parts act upon metal (e.g., grape husks acting upon copper) they coagulate/associate and yield distillates and residues (e.g., an aqua fortis‑like spirit and crocus powder) different from the pure juice; thus distillates should be ascribed to the altered salts rather than assumed to be original vinegars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use residue analysis and careful tracing of prior treatments (burial with metal, calcination) to assign origins of distillates; do not attribute distillate properties naively to original feedstock without considering transformative interactions.
